Empirical Research Plan: “Incumbent‐Party Advantage in U.S. House Elections, 1946–1998”

================================================================
1. Identification Strategy
----------------------------------------------------------------
• Method: Sharp Regression Discontinuity Design (RDD).  
• Justification  
  – Whether the Democratic (versus Republican/other) party holds the seat in Congress for term t+1 is a deterministic step function of whether its candidate won the previous election in that district (vote margin > 0).  
  – Near the zero‐margin cutoff the winner is quasi-random because idiosyncratic shocks (weather, turnout errors, counting noise) dominate strategic factors, so districts just above and just below 0 pp Democratic margin are expected to be comparable on observed and unobserved determinants.  
  – RDD directly answers the causal question: “What is the effect of party incumbency, relative to not holding the seat, on next-cycle outcomes?”  

================================================================
2. Treatment and Control
----------------------------------------------------------------
• Running variable: m_it  = Democratic vote share – 50 (percentage-point Democratic margin) in election t.  
• Cutoff: m_it = 0.  
• Treatment indicator (T_i): 1 = Democrat wins seat in t (m_it > 0), 0 = Democrat loses (m_it ≤ 0).  
• Timing: Treatment is delivered immediately after election t and is “active” during the next cycle (t → t+1).  
• Outcomes measured in election t+1:  
  1. P(Democrat wins t+1)  
  2. Democratic vote share in t+1  
  3. P(same Democratic candidate runs again)  
  4. P(same Democratic candidate runs and wins)  
• Control group: districts with m_it just below 0 (Democrat barely lost, hence Republican is the incumbent party).  

================================================================
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
----------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Continuity of Potential Outcomes at Cutoff  
    – In absence of treatment, expected t+1 outcomes vary smoothly with m_it around 0.  
    – Plausible: no evidence parties can perfectly forecast/tailor to ±½ pp; historical recounts rarely change seat control; vote counts are discrete and noisy.

A2. No Precise Manipulation of Running Variable  
    – Actors cannot sort exactly to win by 0.1 pp versus lose by 0.1 pp.  
    – Plausible in large-scale House races; we will test with McCrary density and covariate balance.

A3. Stable Unit Treatment Value (SUTVA)  
    – Treatment to one district does not affect outcomes in other districts within the estimation bandwidth.  
    – Reasonable; cross-district spillovers are minor relative to noise. (We can cluster s.e. by district-decade.)

================================================================
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation
----------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Manipulation / Fraud near cutoff  
    – Test: McCrary density test; placebo RDs on pre-t covariates (e.g., lag vote share, census traits).  
    – Donut RD: drop |m_it| < 0.25 pp to remove recount outliers.

T2. Redistricting or District Abolition between t and t+1  
    – Already excluded years ending 0 or 2; additionally drop districts whose geographic code changes between t and t+1.  
    – Robustness: restrict to within-decade elections only.

T3. Candidate-Specific Selection (e.g., star challengers run only when race is close)  
    – Include lagged candidate experience controls (past wins, nominations) and test covariate balance.  
    – Falsification: RD on probability that same Republican candidate runs again when Democrat barely wins.

================================================================
5. R Code Outline
----------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# --------------------------------------------------------------
# 0. Packages
# --------------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)      # fast data handling
library(fixest)          # regressions with clustered s.e.
library(rdrobust)        # RD estimation
library(rddensity)       # McCrary density test

# --------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Load and prepare data
# --------------------------------------------------------------
# Assume file 'house_elections_1946_1998.csv' in working dir
dt <- fread("house_elections_1946_1998.csv")

# Basic variable construction
dt[, dem_margin := dem_vote_share - 50]              # pp margin
dt[, treat := as.integer(dem_margin > 0)]            # Dem wins
dt[, abs_margin := abs(dem_margin)]

# Outcomes (already in file or create)
# p_win_tp1 : Democratic victory in t+1
# dem_share_tp1 : Democratic vote share t+1
# cand_runs_again : 1 if same Dem candidate runs t+1
# cand_runs_and_wins : 1 if same Dem candidate runs and wins

# --------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Analysis bandwidth (±5 pp baseline)
# --------------------------------------------------------------
bw0 <- 5
sample <- dt[abs_margin <= bw0 & !redistricting_year]

# --------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Sharp RD using rdrobust – main outcome: win prob
# --------------------------------------------------------------
y <- sample$p_win_tp1
x <- sample$dem_margin
rd_out <- rdrobust(y = y, x = x, c = 0, p = 1, h = bw0)
summary(rd_out)

# --------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Additional outcomes
# --------------------------------------------------------------
rd_share <- rdrobust(sample$dem_share_tp1, x, c = 0, p = 1, h = bw0)
rd_run   <- rdrobust(sample$cand_runs_again, x, c = 0, p = 1, h = bw0)
rd_runwin<- rdrobust(sample$cand_runs_and_wins, x, c = 0, p = 1, h = bw0)

# --------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Density test (manipulation check)
# --------------------------------------------------------------
dens <- rddensity(x, c = 0)
summary(dens)

# --------------------------------------------------------------
# 6. Donut RD robustness: drop |margin| < 0.25 pp
# --------------------------------------------------------------
donut <- sample[abs_margin >= 0.25]
rd_donut <- rdrobust(donut$p_win_tp1, donut$dem_margin, c = 0, p = 1, h = bw0)
summary(rd_donut)

# --------------------------------------------------------------
# 7. Covariate balance check (example: lag Dem share)
# --------------------------------------------------------------
rd_cov <- rdrobust(sample$dem_vote_share_lag1, sample$dem_margin, c = 0, p = 1, h = bw0)
summary(rd_cov)
```

================================================================
6. Expected Results
----------------------------------------------------------------
• Direction: Positive. Holding the seat should raise the Democratic party’s probability of winning the next election and boost its vote share; it should also raise the likelihood that the same Democratic candidate runs and wins again.  
• Magnitude priors (guided by descriptive incumbency patterns):  
  – P(win t+1): +25–35 percentage points.  
  – Vote share t+1: +5–10 pp.  
  – P(same candidate runs): +15 pp; P(runs & wins): +20 pp.

================================================================
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (RDD)
----------------------------------------------------------------
C1. No precise manipulation of running variable …………………  1  
C2. Covariate continuity at cutoff ………………………………………  1  
C3. Correct bandwidth / functional form chosen ………………  0.5  
C4. No other treatment jumps at cutoff ……………………………  1  
C5. Sufficient observations close to cutoff ……………………  1  
Total (out of 5) …………………………………………………… 4.5

================================================================
End of research plan.
